Decision record · Reviewed 20 October 2026

Evidence behind
the product choices.

Keep the existing notes-to-approved-report direction. Test the effort of review, the clarity of the recipient’s next action, and the coordination needed to finish the handoff.

What this evidence establishes: a real correspondence workflow, existing competing solutions, and useful hypotheses to test. Revenue, profit, customer retention, willingness to pay for ReferralFlow, and a reliable forecast of founder income remain unverified.

What we know about the team’s discovery

The uploaded backup describes a specialist interview about correspondence effort and fragmented information. The original interview transcript and the original persona sheets were unavailable in this audit. The current working document describes broader inter-office information problems. None supplies measured time savings or paid demand for this prototype.

Dr. Arjun Patel (specialist), Dr. Elena Ruiz (referring dentist), and Maya Chen (coordinator) are fictional working personas. The role mapping was preserved from the uploaded prototype. Confirm it against the team’s earlier persona submission before presenting it as established semester work.

Scope decisions

Included

Existing fictional notes, editable draft, source comparison, explicit missing information, recipient confirmation, approval tied to the current version, real file export, and clearly labeled local handoff states.

Deferred

Ambient recording, diagnosis, radiograph interpretation, scheduling, claims, broad practice management, marketing, production accounts, actual patient records, live delivery, payment collection and PMS integration.

These additions would widen the experiment. Integration may become necessary if workflow testing shows that copy/export creates too much work.

The commercial decision after this assignment

  1. Observe the current process. Start with accessible specialist practices. Record report volume, software, total staff and clinician time, corrections, handoff delay and the person with purchase authority.
  2. Test the relevant version. Use a fictional or appropriately authorized case. Compare with the practice’s actual template and report process. A is the provisional first conversation because it most directly matches the reported specialist task; that choice can change after observation.
  3. Offer a bounded pilot. Agree the deliverable, recurring price, duration, support and decision criteria with the buyer. Record exactly whether they accepted, paid, used it again and renewed.
  4. Measure the economics. Start with subscription revenue earned for the month, allocating annual prepayments across the service period. Subtract variable model, hosting, delivery, payment and support costs to calculate contribution. Deduct each expense once; subtract remaining acquisition and fixed operating expenses to assess operating profit. Show a separate analytical adjustment for unpaid founder labor at an explicit replacement cost. Cash receipts can differ from revenue.
  5. Advance only on observed value. Repeated task improvement, a paying buyer and repeat use justify further investment. If the current tool is adequate or review/support consumes the benefit, revise that workflow before expanding the product.
Decision today: continue ReferralFlow’s committed product direction and use these prototypes to choose the interaction. A class vote can guide the semester. Evidence from paying practices must guide a commercial launch.

No customer tests, practice outreach, payments, renewals, class votes or team rehearsals are claimed in this package. All case data are fictional. Drafting uses local templates; generation, roles and delivery are simulated.
